newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslavia's 1997 trade gap may widen - institute.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslavia's 1997 trade gap may widen - institute.

text.p: Yugoslavia's trade gap will widen in 1997 unless the government creates a clear export strategy and the country returns to world organisations, economists said on Wednesday.
"There is a lack of strategy for Yugoslav exports and of the economy in general," said Radovan Kovacevic, director of the Belgrade-based Institute for Foreign trade.
The trade deficit last year reached $2.26 billion and rose by another $191 million in January.
"The gap between exports and imports is widening and I am afraid it might even reach $4 billion by the end of this year," said Zivojin Jevtic, a leading economist with the institute.
Trade slowed in January, with imports down to $323 million from the previous month's $396 million, and exports to $132 million from $168 million.
"This trend has continued since last October and is linked with an overall slowdown in industrial activity, which can be expected to drop further," Kovacevic said.
Although January year-on-year industrial output rose 2.9 percent, it dropped by 20.8 percent against last December.
"Seasonally adjusted data shows definite stagnation, and without increased productivity we cannot hope to raise exports," Jevtic said.
Kovacevic said a major turnabout in the structure of exports should not be expected this year because Yugoslav industry was not equipped for it.
The largest exporters last year were agriculture, food, metal processing, ferrous and non-ferrous metallurgy, and chemical industry, accounting for 80 percent of exports.
Sectors such as tourism and construction, significant hard currency earners before the breakup of former Yugoslavia in 1991, will remain low earners this year, he said.
The government said it planned to boost 1997 exports by 42 percent and imports by 20 percent while keeping the trade gap close to $2 billion.

Although international sanctions against Yugoslavia, comprising Serbia and Montenegro, were lifted in October 1995, an "outer wall" remained in place barring it access to international organisations and desperately needed funds to revive its devastated economy.
U.S. Charge D'Affaires Richard Miles on Wednesday dampened hopes the outer wall would be removed soon.

"As long as Yugoslavia does not fulfill certain conditions, it will not be allowed to participate in the work of the United Nations and other international organisations, to join the International Monetary Fund, World Bank or other financial institutions," Miles told a seminar on international relations in Belgrade.

The conditions include democratisation, improvement of human rights in the majority Albanian province of Kosovo, full cooperation with The Hague war crimes tribunal and progress in talks on succession with other former Yugoslav republics. -- Amra Kevic, Belgrade newsroom +381 11 2224305
